props.title: The Jolson Story
props.initialSlug: Landmark biopic of America's first superstar singer

sections.content: The Jolson Story (1946) marks a pivotal moment in Hollywood's treatment of both musical biopics and Jewish representation. Larry Parks delivers an electrifying performance as Al Jolson, capturing the legendary performer's magnetic stage presence and controversial blackface performances. The film set the template for musical biopics that would influence everything from Night and Day (1946) to Walk the Line (2005), establishing core genre elements like the rise-to-fame narrative, relationship struggles, and recreations of iconic performances. Despite sanitizing aspects of Jolson's life, the film's technical achievements in Technicolor and sound mixing were groundbreaking.

sections.content: The film's handling of Jolson's Jewish identity and use of blackface performances reflects Hollywood's complex navigation of racial and ethnic representation in the 1940s. While Gentleman's Agreement (1947) would directly confront antisemitism the following year, The Jolson Story takes a more subtle approach, depicting Jolson's cantorial roots while downplaying potential controversies. The film's massive success spawned a sequel, Jolson Sings Again (1949), and influenced later Jewish-themed musicals like Funny Girl (1968).

Larry Parks' mimicry of Jolson's performing style, combined with Jolson's own voice on the soundtrack, created a fascinating hybrid performance that anticipated later dubbing techniques. This approach would be echoed in biopics like The Great Caruso (1951) and much later in La Bamba (1987), where actors lip-synced to the original artists' recordings. sections.content: The film's structure established enduring biopic conventions: the protagonist's humble beginnings, discovery of talent, rise to fame, personal conflicts, and ultimate triumph. This formula would be repeated in countless music biopics, from Coal Miner's Daughter (1980) to Ray (2004). The Jolson Story's innovative use of Technicolor to capture theatrical performances influenced how musicals would be filmed for decades.
